paper_metadata.title: Powder bed fusion additive manufacturing of Ni-based superalloys: a review of the main microstructural constituents and characterization techniques

evidence.quote: Metal additive manufacturing (AM) has unlocked unique opportunities for making complex Ni-based superalloy parts

attributes.composition: Ni with Co, Fe, Cr, Mo, W, V, Ti, Al

evidence.section: Overview of main microstructure constituents in common Ni-based superalloys
evidence.quote: The primary matrix phase in Ni-based superalloys is the face centered cubic (FCC) c.

attributes.morphology: spherical to cuboidal with increased aging

evidence.section: Overview of main microstructure constituents in common Ni-based superalloys
evidence.quote: The c0 phase is an FCC-like L1 2 ordered phase of the composition Ni 3X, where X is primarily the element Al [39], however Ti and Ta can often replace the Al in c0 when present [40]. With increased aging, c0 transforms from spherical to cuboidal shape [39].

evidence.section: Overview of main microstructure constituents in common Ni-based superalloys
evidence.quote: The c00 phase is a body centered tetragonal (BCT) ordered D0 22 phase with a chemical composition of Ni3Nb [39]. Typically, c00 forms as plate-like particles.

evidence.section: Overview of main microstructure constituents in common Ni-based superalloys
evidence.quote: Due to its meta-stable behavior, c00 will transform to d with an orthorhombic D0 a structure above * 885 /C176 C[39].

evidence.section: Overview of main microstructure constituents in common Ni-based superalloys
evidence.quote: Topology closed-packed (TCP) phases are less desirable and often occur due to the high number of elements found in Ni-based superalloys. These include R, P, l, Laves, and r.

evidence.section: Overview of main microstructure constituents in common Ni-based superalloys
evidence.quote: Depending on the detailed composition, carbides such as MC, M6C, M7C3, and M23C6 may form, which may help to strengthen Ni-based superalloys further through exerting grain boundary pinning if present in suitable quantity and dispersion.

evidence.section: Review of solidification and solid-state phase transformations and context in AM
evidence.quote: if the solid–liquid interface is moving fast enough, non-equilibrium solidification conditions may occur where the solute diffusing away from the interface can become trapped in the solid. This is known as solute trapping [53].

evidence.section: Review of solidification and solid-state phase transformations and context in AM
evidence.quote: During solidification, the partitioning of elements occurs due to differences in equilibrium composition between the solid and the liquid phases.

evidence.section: Review of solidification and solid-state phase transformations and context in AM
evidence.quote: Faster solidification rates reduce Laves formation due to trapping of Nb in the matrix phase [54].
